context_before.text: In order to investigate the corrosion behavior of the high temperature HAZ, which is heated to1350 Cor higher, the specimens were heated in Ar gas by an induction heating machine. The temperature of the heat pattern shown in Figure 2 was measured by a thermocouple, which directly contacted the surface of the specimen.

The pitting potential was measured potentiodynamically in 5% NaCl deaerated solution at 60 C at a sweep rate of 20 mV/min with a potentiostat. The (reference) SCE and the platinum counter electrode were used in this study. The test specimen, a disk 15 mm in diameter and 2 mm in thickness, was polished with No. 600 emery paper, washed with water and alcohol, and then degreased with acetone. The potential at which the anodic current density increases dramatically by the occurrence of pitting was adopted as the pitting potential (Vc’).

context_after.text: Pitting corrosion tests in $\mathsf { F e C l } _ { 3 }$ aerated solution were also conducted by the measurement of the CPT of the materials using 25 x 50 x 2 mm specimens polished with No. 600 emery paper. The pitting corrosion resistance was evaluated by the highest temperature below which the material did not suffer pitting corrosion attack after a 24 h exposure in 10 wt% $F e C l _ { 3 }$ 6H2O solution in water. The solution temperature was increased by 2.5 C until the CPT was reached. The criteria of this test was used for the determination of the presence of pits.

Uniaxial constant load SCC tests were conducted in a 15 L autoclave with a lever-type loading system, as shown in Figure 3. The constant load SCC test specimen had a nominal gage length of 20 mm and a diameter of 3 mm. The autoclave was purged with nitrogen to deaerate the solution, and then the vacuum was applied. Finally, the autoclave was purged with ${ \sf H } _ { 2 } { \sf S }$ and pressurized to the desired partial pressure before heating. SCC resistance was evaluated by the time to failure in 20% NaCl solution with 1 atm (101 kPa) H2S at 100 C. The U-bend SCC tests were also performed in 20% NaCl solution with 10 atm (1010 kPa) $\mathtt { C O } _ { 2 }$ and 0 to 0.1 atm (0 to 10.1 kPa) ${ \mathsf { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathsf { S } }$ at 100 C.

context_after.text: In order to investigate the effect of nitrogen content on the corrosion behavior of the high temperature HAZ, i.e., HAZ(B) in Figure 4, the materials were heated with the simulated heat pattern shown in Figure 2. Figure 15 shows the effect of peak temperature at heat cycle on SCC susceptibility of 22%Cr duplex SS containing 0.14% nitrogen. SCC occurs only at the peak temperature of 1375 C. That microstructure with various peak temperatures is shown in Figure 16. The duplex phase transforms to single α-phase when the peak temperature exceeds 1350 C and then needle-shaped γ-phase precipitates during the cooling process. Therefore, the peak temperature of 1375 C was selected for the investigation of the effect of nitrogen content on the corrosion behavior of HAZ(B).

Figure 17 gives the effect of nitrogen content on intergranular corrosion of simulated HAZ(B) of 22%Cr duplex SSs. The alloys with nitrogen content below 0.077% suffer the intergranular attacks in the Strauss and Huey tests. The high sensitivity to intergranular corrosion of 0.077% or lower nitrogen alloys, whose structure is single α-phase after heating, results from the formation of the chromium depleted zone along α/α grain boundaries by the precipitation of ${ \tt C r } _ { 2 3 } { \tt C } _ { 6 }$ and/or $C r _ { 2 } N.$

section_title.text: Corrosion Resistance of High Temperature HAZ

context_before.text: In order to investigate the effect of nitrogen content on the corrosion behavior of the high temperature HAZ, i.e., HAZ(B) in Figure 4, the materials were heated with the simulated heat pattern shown in Figure 2. Figure 15 shows the effect of peak temperature at heat cycle on SCC susceptibility of 22%Cr duplex SS containing 0.14% nitrogen. SCC occurs only at the peak temperature of 1375 C. That microstructure with various peak temperatures is shown in Figure 16. The duplex phase transforms to single α-phase when the peak temperature exceeds 1350 C and then needle-shaped γ-phase precipitates during the cooling process. Therefore, the peak temperature of 1375 C was selected for the investigation of the effect of nitrogen content on the corrosion behavior of HAZ(B).

Figure 17 gives the effect of nitrogen content on intergranular corrosion of simulated HAZ(B) of 22%Cr duplex SSs. The alloys with nitrogen content below 0.077% suffer the intergranular attacks in the Strauss and Huey tests. The high sensitivity to intergranular corrosion of 0.077% or lower nitrogen alloys, whose structure is single α-phase after heating, results from the formation of the chromium depleted zone along α/α grain boundaries by the precipitation of ${ \tt C r } _ { 2 3 } { \tt C } _ { 6 }$ and/or $C r _ { 2 } N.$

context_after.text: It is indicated in Figure 18 that nitrogen is beneficial in the improvement of the pitting resistance in NaCl solution, as well as in $F e C l _ { 3 }$ solution. If the CPT value in the $\mathsf { F e C l } _ { 3 }$ solution is required to be more than 30 C at HAZ(B), a 0.14% or higher nitrogen content is necessary for a 22%Cr, 5.5%Ni, and 3%Mo base composition. The pitting potential and the CPT of the simulated HAZ(B) with a high nitrogen of 0.238% are lower than those of the base metal shown in Figures 6 and 7.

Figure 19 shows SCC test results in 20% NaCI solution with 1 atm (101 ${ \sf k P a }) \sf H _ { 2 } S$ at 100 C. The SCC susceptibility of the simulated HAZ(B) is greater than that of the base metal shown in Figure 8. The materials suffer SCC in a short time under the high applied stress of 441 MPa. When the applied stress is decreased to 343 MPa, the alloys containing more than 0.123% nitrogen sustain the resistance to cracking. The alioys below the nitrogen content of 0.077%, which have the almost single α-phase, have high sensitivity to SCC even under the low applied stress of 343 MPa.

SCC occurs on all materials in the condition of 0.1 atm (10.1 kPa) ${ \mathsf H } _ { 2 } { \mathsf S } + { \mathsf 1 } 0$ atm (1010 kPa) ${ \mathsf { C O } } _ { 2 }$. In the condition of 10 atm (1010 kPa) ${ \mathsf { C O } } _ { 2 }$ the cracks of the alloy with 0.047% nitrogen content, which is sensitive to intergranular corrosion mentioned above, are intergranular, which is considered to propagate along the chromium-depleted zone at the α/α grain boundaries.

In the condition of 10 atm (1010 kPa) ${ \mathsf { C O } } _ { 2 }$ the cracks of the alloy with 0.047% nitrogen content, which is sensitive to intergranular corrosion mentioned above, are intergranular, which is considered to propagate along the chromium-depleted zone at the α/α grain boundaries.

It has been shown that nitrogen is beneficial in improving the pitting corrosion resistance of the base metal. This beneficial effect of nitrogen can be attributed to improving the pitting corrosion resistant of the austenite phase, as discussed below. Chromium and molybdenum contents in the ferrite and austenite phases are almost constant independent of nitrogen content, as shown in Figure 21. The austenite phase has ~21%Cr-2.5%Mo, while the ferrite phase has 23%Cr-3.5%Mo. Assuming that the pitting index equation is $\complement \pm$ 3Mo + 16N (as proposed in Reference 9) and that the nitrogen exists only in the austenite phase of 60%, as shown in Figure 1, the nitrogen content required to get the same pitting corrosion resistance in austenite phase as that in the ferrite phase is ~0.18%. Therefore, the pitting corrosion is thought to initiate at the austenite phase below the nítrogen content of 0.18% from this rough estimation. Figure 22 shows the microscopic observation of pitting initiation of the 22%Cr duplex SS in NaCi solution. In the alloys with nitrogen contents of $0. 1 3 7 \%$ pitting corrosion is observed to initiate in austenite phase. When the nitrogen content increases to 0.164%, it can be seen that pitting occurs at random on the ferrite and austenite phases. The estimation mentioned above almost agrees with the observation.

context_after.text: Thus, the role of nitrogen to the increase in pitting corrosion resistance is attributed to the improvement of the austenite phase of the duplex SS.

It was observed that nitrogen content has little effect on intergranular corrosion of the materials aged at the temperature around 700 C in the Huey test, which suggests that the determining factor of this corrosion may be primarily the precipitation of ${ \mathsf { C r } } _ { 2 3 } { \mathsf { C } } _ { 6 }.$ In fact, the precipitation of $C r _ { 2 3 } C _ { 6 }$ was observed at the $\alpha / \gamma$ and α/α grain boundaries.
